what.text: Latanoprost is a prostaglandin F2α analogue. As an eye drop it lowers pressure inside the eye.
The eye-drop label lists changes to the eyelashes as a known effect: longer, thicker, darker and more lashes. That effect is why it has been tried on scalp hair.
Using latanoprost for hair loss is off-label.

research.text: Two small pilot trials have tested latanoprost on scalp hair. A larger trial of a different combination product is under way, with no results yet. None has tested a compounded combination spray.

research.title: Latanoprost 0.1% on two small scalp zones

facts.v: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot. Each man had one zone treated with latanoprost and one with placebo.
16 men with mild pattern hair loss (Hamilton II–III)
Hair growth, density, diameter, pigmentation and anagen/telogen ratio

research.found: Hair density was higher on the latanoprost zone than at the start and than on the placebo zone at 24 weeks. The authors note only young men with mild hair loss took part, and the results may not apply to others.

src.label: Blume-Peytavi et al., J Am Acad Dermatol, 2012

research.title: Latanoprost acid in women with pattern hair loss

facts.v: Randomized, double-blind, dose-ranging pilot, one center
29 women: 2 on vehicle, 27 on one of three strengths of latanoprost acid
Change in hair count in a target area; scalp-imaging signs

research.found: Hair counts rose in all three active groups, with no significant difference between them. No serious side effects were reported. Three authors hold a patent on this use. The authors say larger trials are needed.

research.text: This trial used latanoprost acid, a different form from the latanoprost in the eye drop.

research.title: TH07: minoxidil, finasteride and latanoprost solution

facts.v: Phase III, randomized, triple-blind, multicenter; TH07 compared with minoxidil 5% and with placebo
Men with pattern hair loss; 420 planned

research.found: Recruiting. No results have been posted. The sponsor is a company, Triple Hair Inc.

us.text: FDA approved Xalatan (latanoprost 0.005% eye drops) in 1996. It is not approved for hair loss.
Compounded drugs are not FDA approved. FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

src.label: FDA, Compounding and the FDA: Q&A

us.text: Xalatan’s approved use is lowering raised eye pressure in people with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.
Latanoprost is FDA approved only as eye drops. Compounded hair sprays that contain it are not FDA approved.
No latanoprost product is FDA approved for hair loss.

world.lead: Latanoprost is an approved eye-pressure medicine in the US, Canada and EU countries. No regulator we checked has approved it for hair loss.

countries.status: Approved medicine (Xalatan, 1996, raised eye pressure). Prescription-only. Not approved for hair loss.
Xalatan is marketed and listed as a prescription drug. Not approved for hair loss.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Latanoprost is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List or on the 2027 List, which takes effect January 1, 2027.

side.text: Side effects below come from the Xalatan eye-drop label. No label covers use on the scalp.

items.text: Darker iris, eyelid skin and eyelashes. The iris change is likely to be permanent.
Longer, thicker and more eyelashes; usually reversible.
Eye inflammation (iritis or uveitis) and swelling of the retina (macular edema).
In trials: foreign-body feeling, stinging, red eye, blurred vision and spotty corneal irritation.

side.text: In the 2026 scalp trial, no serious side effects were reported.

unconfirmed: We could not confirm latanoprost’s UK status from an MHRA record; the MHRA products site did not load without scripts.
We could not reach Australia’s TGA (ARTG search failed), so Australia is pending.
We could not open the Drugs@FDA website itself; the approval date comes from FDA’s openFDA copy of Drugs@FDA.
surprises: The hair-growth idea comes from a side effect: FDA’s Xalatan label lists eyelash growth as an unwanted effect of the eye drops, not as an approved use.
The only trial in women used latanoprost acid, not the latanoprost in the eye drop, and three of its authors hold a patent on that use.
